Moon jellyfish
Aurelia aurita

Aurelia aurita is a translucent scyphozoan, or true jellyfish, whose familiar saucer-shaped medusa is only one part of its life cycle. Once treated as cosmopolitan, the species was later separated from many similar Aurelia; A. aurita is now reported mainly from the northeastern Atlantic, with introduced populations in northeastern US and Argentina, though natural arrival in the US remains possible.
A typical adult bell is about 25–40 cm across. Four horseshoe-shaped gonads show through it, above four oral arms and fine marginal tentacles; the clear body may have a faint blue or pink tint.
The medusa lives in pelagic water; its polyp is benthic and attaches to a hard surface, often under shelter in shallow brackish sites.

Tentacles and bell mucus intercept zooplankton, including copepods and small larvae. Cnidocytes are stinging cells containing nematocysts, tiny capsules that fire venomous harpoons when prey touches a tentacle. The same contact-triggered discharge can stun predators, so these cells serve defense as well as feeding. Cilia carry captured food along the oral arms to the mouth and gastrovascular cavity for digestion.
Bell pulses propel the medusa briefly, while currents carry it farther. Medusae may gather to breed; attached polyps bud asexually.

Adults have separate sexes; males release sperm, and fertilized eggs develop in brood pockets on female oral arms. The ciliated planula swims briefly before settling and becoming a small attached polyp, or scyphistoma. The polyp may bud, then strobilate: constrictions segment it and release disc-shaped ephyrae. Ephyrae develop into adult medusae. Seasonal temperature affects strobilation timing.
Podocysts, protective resting cysts produced by polyps, help them endure food shortages and resist nudibranch predation during the benthic stage.
Periodic local blooms can strand jellies on beaches or clog coastal seawater intakes, creating a local infrastructure problem rather than evidence of a global population decline.

Moose
Alces alces

The moose is the largest living deer, inhabiting northern forests of North America and Eurasia, from Alaska and Canada to Scandinavia, Russia, northern China and Mongolia. In British English it is often called elk.

A shoulder hump, heavy body, long legs and drooping muzzle define its shape. Only males grow annual antlers: broad palms are common in North America, narrower forms occur in Eurasia. Coat colour ranges from brown to nearly black. Long legs cross deep snow; nostrils close underwater, aiding submerged feeding.

Moose favour northern woodland, young forest, wetlands and shores. In Alaska they use river corridors, timberline plateaus and burns where willow, birch and aspen regrow. Lakes and marshes offer food and cover. Seasonal movements link feeding, calving, rutting and wintering areas.

Food varies with season and supply. In summer it eats leaves, herbs and shallow-water plants; spring also brings grazing. Woody shoots, especially willow, birch and aspen, matter more in autumn and winter. Its long muzzle and closable nostrils help crop submerged plants.

Moose are usually solitary; cows stay with calves, and adults meet more during the autumn rut. Males push antlers against rivals; winners may mate with several females. Seasonal movements vary locally. Daily activity centres on feeding, resting and rumination.

In Alaska, mating peaks in late September and early October. After about 230 days, females calve in spring, usually producing one calf; twins occur in favourable conditions. Calves grow quickly, nurse through summer and are usually weaned in autumn, remaining with their mother into the next year.

Browsing shrubs, saplings and aquatic plants affects forest regeneration. At unusually high density in Forillon, Parks Canada documents major vegetation changes. That local case shows how abundant moose can shape plant communities; effects vary with population and habitat.

The global IUCN assessment (last assessed 27 September 2015; published 2016) classed moose as Least Concern, with an increasing overall trend. It cited habitat alteration as a major human threat. This dated assessment is not a current survey of regional populations.

Mugger crocodile
Crocodylus palustris

The mugger, or marsh crocodile, is a broad-snouted crocodilian native to South Asia and eastern Iran. It occupies freshwater rivers, lakes, marshes and ponds, including reservoirs and irrigation waters. This adaptable predator persists in both protected wetlands and human-altered waterways.

Males usually stay below 3.5 m; females average 2.5–3 m, though exceptional individuals approach 5 m. The mugger has the broadest snout in Crocodylus. Adults are grey-brown; young have lighter colouring and dark bands. Its muscular tail drives swimming, and sturdy limbs support movement on land. Crocodilians can also lift the body into a high walk, though fast gaits are poorly documented for this species. Hatchlings measure about 25–27 cm.

Muggers inhabit freshwater rivers, lakes, marshes and ponds, often using deeper pools with sandy banks and dense riverside cover. They also occupy reservoirs, irrigation canals and aquaculture ponds; some enter brackish lagoons. This flexibility allows use of human-made waters, but can bring crocodiles near fishing and farming communities.

Muggers are opportunistic carnivores whose diet changes with size. Young take insects, crustaceans and small fish; adults eat fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Deer and buffalo are occasional large prey, not a routine meal for every crocodile. Local feeding reflects available prey and body size; individuals have also been seen corralling fish.

As ectotherms, muggers warm by basking and cool by entering water or shade. Individuals dig bank burrows that buffer harsh heat and cold; underground temperatures change more slowly than surface air. During prolonged hot, dry spells, a mugger may aestivate—remain inactive in its burrow—then travel overland when seeking permanent water. Such treks can cross roads and railways.

Females lay 10–30 eggs in a hole nest, often in sandy bank soil; some nests sit beside or inside burrows. Dry-season laying varies geographically. Eggs incubate for about 55–75 days. Temperature affects sex: controlled experiments yielded all females at 28–31 °C and all males at 32.5 °C, with both sexes at intermediate temperatures. The female guards the nest and may help hatchlings emerge and carry them to water; field observations document such care, but its duration and effect on survival remain uncertain. Captive double clutches have not been documented in the wild.

As a generalist predator, the mugger links aquatic and terrestrial prey in wetland food webs; its eggs and young are also eaten by other animals. In the Chambal River, a 2024 study found increasing mugger numbers and occupancy in a sanctuary established for gharial recovery. Researchers flagged possible competition with this more habitat-specialised crocodilian as a local management concern, not a proven species-wide effect.

The global IUCN assessment dated 30 June 2009 and published in 2013 classified the mugger as Vulnerable (A2cd). The IUCN Crocodile Specialist Group estimated over 20,000 adults in its 2025 action plan. Habitat loss, fishing nets, egg collection, persecution and transport deaths remain documented threats. A 2008–2010 survey near Vadodara documented crocodile rescues and relocation after human encounters, illustrating the need for local coexistence measures.

Striped Red Mullet
Mullus surmuletus

The striped red mullet is a goatfish of the north-eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Like all goatfishes it has two barbels under the chin, which it uses to find food in the sediment. It is a warm-temperate species that reaches its northern limit in the North Sea.

The body is marked with longitudinal red and brown stripes, and the first dorsal fin has dark markings. The barbels are longer than the pectoral fin and fold into a groove on the throat. In the North Sea it may reach 40 cm and 1 kg; in the Mediterranean males reach about 23 cm and females about 34 cm.

It ranges from western Norway and the English Channel south to Senegal and the Canary Islands, and through the Mediterranean and Black Sea. In the Channel and North Sea it lives at 3–90 m on sandy or muddy bottoms, sometimes on rock; in the western Mediterranean it is found mainly at 10–50 m on rough bottoms.

It uses its barbels to detect food in soft bottoms and may dig a pit with its mouth to seize prey. Its food is almost entirely bottom-living animals: shrimps, amphipods, polychaete worms, molluscs and small bottom fishes.

In the north it is a seasonal visitor: it enters the southern North Sea through the Channel in spring, travels along the continental coast as far as the Skagerrak and Kattegat, and returns to the Channel in autumn. Young fish live at the surface, then move to the coast and take up a bottom-living life.

Eggs and larvae are pelagic. Spawning occurs in May–June off southern Brittany and May–July off Plymouth, but mainly April–September, with a peak in July, in the northern Aegean Sea. In the Channel and North Sea fish are reported to mature after one year. At about 5 cm the young leave the surface, move toward the coast and take on adult colours.

Young fish are blue-backed and silvery and feed at the surface on larval crustaceans and copepods. Adults feed on the bottom. Winter catches in the North Sea have grown quickly since the late 1980s, and young fish have been found there, suggesting spawning may now occur in the southern North Sea.

The IUCN classed the species as Least Concern in 2014 (as reported by FishBase). It is a valuable commercial fish in the southern Bay of Biscay and Iberian waters, where it is caught in large numbers.

Murray cod
Maccullochella peelii

The Murray cod is a large freshwater predator endemic to eastern Australia. Unlike true cod, it belongs to Percichthyidae, alongside the related trout cod and eastern freshwater cod. It is Australia’s largest freshwater fish.

Its robust, elongated body carries a broad, flattened head, small eyes and a wide mouth with fine teeth; the snout profile is concave. Adults commonly measure under 70 cm, while exceptional historical fish reached about 1.8 m and 113.5 kg. Olive-green flanks bear darker marbling and fade to a pale belly. Rounded fins frame a long dorsal fin with a notch between spiny and soft parts. The mouth reaches behind the eyes; the lower jaw may protrude. Maximum lifespan estimates range from 75 to 114 years.

Deep pools, boulders, undercut banks and submerged fallen timber provide ambush cover and shelter. The fish is most characteristic of lowland rivers, though it also occurs in some upland reaches. Its native range spans the Murray–Darling Basin in Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria and South Australia, excluding the coldest upper reaches.

Adults take crayfish, freshwater shrimp and fish, including introduced carp and redfin when available; molluscs and occasionally small animals from the water’s edge broaden the menu. It hunts by ambush from cover.
Territorial, it favors deep pools beside logs, boulders or overhanging banks. By day it shelters; at night it may hunt shallows or the surface.

Maturity usually comes at about five years, though growth and location alter the timing. In spring, pairs court and choose hard surfaces, often submerged logs or rocks. The female lays eggs on this submerged surface; the male fertilises them externally. The male guards and fans the eggs until free-swimming larvae hatch. The larvae drift away, use their yolk reserves, then feed on tiny invertebrates as they develop.
A top predator, it eats native fish, crustaceans and introduced carp in the same river food webs.

Overfishing sharply reduced stocks from the nineteenth century; dams, altered flows, cold releases and snag removal still damage habitat and recruitment. The species is listed as Vulnerable under Australia’s EPBC Act; this national conservation status is distinct from local fishing regulations.

Spotted Flycatcher
Muscicapa striata

The spotted flycatcher is a small, grey-brown, long-winged songbird that hunts flying insects from a perch. It is one of the latest summer visitors to Britain and winters in Africa, and its numbers there have collapsed over decades.

About the size of a robin, an adult weighs roughly 14.5 g and has a wing length near 86 mm. The back, head, wings and tail are grey-brown and the underparts pale buff with brown streaking on the breast; the name is a misnomer, as it is more streaked than spotted. The sexes look alike; juveniles are spotty and greyer.
It lives in woodland, mature gardens and parks with many trees, and in mature hedgerows with trees on farmland. In Britain and Ireland it breeds throughout except in the far north and west.
It eats flying insects such as flies, butterflies, wasps and craneflies. It watches from a high perch, darts out to catch one in the air, and often returns to the same spot.

It typically arrives in late April or May and leaves in September. Birds tracked by BTO researchers have wintered as far south as Namibia, some 7,000 km from their breeding site. The call is a repetitive, high-pitched tzee and the song a series of scratchy warbles.

The open cup nest is placed on ledges in and around buildings or on creepers against walls and trees. In Britain the first clutch averages 6 June, with typically two broods of four or five eggs. The female alone incubates for 13–14 days and the chicks fledge after about 13–16 days. Breeding typically starts at one year.

Birds, especially jays, cause most nest predation: in a nest-camera study they accounted for 17 of 20 events. Nests in gardens fledged about twice as many chicks as those in woodland or farmland. A typical adult lives about two years; the oldest ringed bird reached eight.

The IUCN Red List classes it as Least Concern, but in the UK it is Red-listed. The breeding population was about 42,000 territories in 2016 and fell by 92% between 1967 and 2024; it has also declined across Europe since 1980. Falling first-year survival seems the main driver, but the ecological cause remains uncertain.

Muskrat
Ondatra zibethicus

The muskrat is a medium-sized rodent of fresh and brackish wetlands, with an insulating coat and aquatic adaptations for foraging among emergent plants and retreating to shelters with underwater entrances. Native to North America, it has also established introduced populations across parts of Europe and Asia.

Adults have a head-and-body length of about 23–33 cm, a tail 18–30 cm, and a mass of roughly 0.7–1.9 kg; size varies among populations. The tail is nearly naked, scaly and compressed from side to side, about as long as the head and body. Stiff hairs fringe the toes, and the hind toes are partly webbed; small ears sit almost hidden in dense brown fur. Unlike the much larger beaver, it has a narrow, laterally flattened tail; nutria are far heavier and have a rounded tail with conspicuous pale whiskers.

Muskrats use marshes, ponds, lakes, streams, drainage canals and estuarine wetlands where water and food remain available. Dense stands of cattails, bulrushes, sedges or reeds provide both edible shoots and cover, while open water lets them travel between feeding and resting sites. In Texas, shallow marshes with stable water around 15–60 cm supported especially favorable conditions; that local range should not be treated as a universal requirement. Houses of cut marsh vegetation rise above water, whereas animals along rivers and canals may excavate bank burrows with underwater entrances.

The diet consists mostly of aquatic plants, especially roots, rhizomes and lower stems of cattails, sedges, bulrushes and water lilies. Strong incisors cut this vegetation, and lips that close behind the incisors allow the animal to gnaw while submerged without taking water into its mouth. It often carries plant pieces to a feeding platform or shelter to eat. Animal food is occasional rather than the norm: documented items include crayfish, mussels, frogs, fish and small turtles, particularly when plant food is scarce. A large, compartmentalized cecum retains fibrous food for microbial fermentation, helping process its plant-heavy diet.

Muskrats are active throughout the day but often become most active from mid-afternoon into dusk. Family members may share a lodge, but crowding and breeding-season competition can cause aggression; scent from musk glands and squeaks or squeals provide communication. In winter, animals in icy regions dig for submerged roots and may build a protective feeding shelter over a hole in the ice.

The breeding season shifts with latitude; in Indiana, most litters arrive in May and June, and females may produce two to four litters per year. After about 28–30 days of gestation, a female gives birth in a grass- or cattail-lined nest, commonly to around six kits. They are born blind and helpless, begin swimming at roughly ten days, and can eat green plants at about three weeks. The mother nurses them until weaning at three to four weeks; young may remain with her longer, especially in the final litter of the season. A two-season field study found that male care varied with mating strategy, and juvenile survival in that study did not depend on the amount of paternal care.

Muskrats are prey for mink, otters, foxes, coyotes, owls, hawks and other wetland predators, linking plant production to higher trophic levels. Their grazing and the vegetation they pile into lodges or feeding platforms can open dense marsh stands into a mosaic of channels, grazed patches and emergent cover. This effect depends on local density and plant growth: heavy grazing can strip vegetation or weaken banks, while moderate activity creates structural variety. Lodges can also be used by other wetland animals as nesting or resting sites.

The global IUCN assessment completed on 20 August 2016 classified the species as Least Concern, citing its broad range and lack of major global threats; this is not a current census of every population. A 42-year analysis of harvest records from 37 U.S. states found evidence of decline from 1970 to 2012 after accounting for pelt prices, with a steeper trend in the Southeast; harvest data remain an indirect measure. The European Union’s consolidated regulation of 7 August 2025 still lists the muskrat as an invasive alien species of Union concern. It was added to that list by Commission Implementing Regulation 2017/1263 in 2017. Burrowing can damage dikes and banks, and intense grazing can alter wetlands, so European management addresses local ecological and infrastructure impacts.

European Mink
Mustela lutreola

The European mink is a semi-aquatic mustelid tied to riverbanks and wetlands. Once widespread across Europe, it now survives in a few isolated populations and is classified as Critically Endangered, one of the most threatened carnivores on the continent.

A medium-sized mustelid with a long body, short legs and a short tail, measuring roughly 32–50 cm from head to tail and weighing from about half a kilogram to a little over one kilogram, males being larger. The coat is glossy brown to almost black. White patches cover both the upper and lower lips, whereas the American mink has white only on the lower lip and chin.

It needs riverbanks for both food and shelter, and lives along small and medium rivers, streams, swamps, riparian forest and wet meadows; large river deltas such as the Danube’s are important. It digs its own burrow, uses an abandoned water vole burrow or shelters among tree roots.

It is a generalist predator of amphibians, small mammals, fish, birds and aquatic invertebrates. Amphibians were long thought to dominate its diet, but data from the Danube Delta do not support this: what it eats varies with the season and the environment.
The European mink is solitary, adults pairing only in the breeding season. It is most active around dusk and before dawn.

Mating takes place from late February to March, and females do not delay pregnancy. Gestation lasts 35–42 days and a litter holds three to seven kits, raised by the female alone. Young are weaned at about ten weeks and become sexually mature at roughly one year.

As a predator of aquatic and semi-aquatic animals, it sits in riverside food webs. Its main current rival is the introduced American mink, which competes with it directly for the same riverbank habitat.

It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List and occupies less than a fifth of its former range, in isolated populations in northern Spain and south-western France, the Danube Delta and parts of Russia. A small population has been re-established on Hiiumaa Island in Estonia. Where American mink are absent, habitat destruction and persecution for its fur remain the main threats. It is protected under the EU Habitats Directive and is extinct in the Czech Republic.

Mute Swan
Cygnus olor
The Mute Swan is a large Eurasian waterfowl of lakes, slow rivers, marshes and sheltered coasts, feeding and nesting close to water.

Adults are white, with black legs, a bright orange bill and a black knob at its base; typical birds measure 127–152 cm long, with a wingspan of 208–238 cm. Males are generally larger than females, although the sexes look alike. Young cygnets are downy and pale grey, with dark bills and legs; older juveniles may show brown-grey feathers as their plumage gradually turns white during the first year. The orange bill and black knob distinguish this species from the Whooper Swan (Cygnus cygnus) and Tundra Swan (Cygnus columbianus), whose bills lack that knob. Both sexes bear the fleshy black knob; it is usually larger in males and varies seasonally, peaking near hatching in one monitored population, so size alone cannot reliably determine sex.
It uses freshwater and brackish wetlands, including ponds, lakes, estuaries and sheltered bays, nesting on islands or vegetated banks near water.

Aquatic vegetation is the main food, though Mute Swans also take animal prey such as snails, insects and small aquatic animals. They skim plants from the surface, tip forward to reach submerged growth and rake the bottom with their feet to uncover tubers. In the eastern Gulf of Finland, one study found a seasonal shift from stranded filamentous algae in late winter to new plant growth during egg laying and incubation.

In one Midlands study, 85% of paired breeders retained the same mate from year to year if both survived. During nesting, pairs defend nest territories with raised-wing displays and arched necks. Though called mute, the swan is not silent: it hisses and snorts when disturbed and gives muffled calls during territorial encounters. After breeding, adults shed all their flight feathers at once and cannot fly for roughly six to eight weeks.

Pairs build a large nest from reeds and other plants; males choose the site and begin the platform, while females shape the cup. British records give a typical clutch of four to seven eggs, usually incubated by the female for about 34–44 days. Newly hatched cygnets can move around the nest, feed and enter the water once their down dries. British records report a typical fledging duration of 120–150 days.

Grazing submerged vegetation can change the biomass and structure of shallow plant beds, although effects vary with local conditions. In an Illinois experiment, swan access was associated with lower below-ground plant biomass, while above-ground biomass did not differ detectably. In Chesapeake Bay, introduced Mute Swans (Cygnus olor) remain year-round, unlike Tundra Swans (Cygnus columbianus), which migrate there for winter. Across Europe, populations are generally resident, although cold weather can displace birds locally.

BirdLife International’s 2016 global IUCN Red List assessment classified the Mute Swan as Least Concern. The species is native across much of Eurasia and introduced in North America. Locally dense introduced flocks can compete with native waterbirds and affect aquatic vegetation. In Britain, population recovery followed severe declines associated with lead poisoning from swallowed fishing weights and shot; restrictions on lead weights and improved protection helped recovery.

Blue Mussel
Mytilus edulis

The blue mussel is a bivalve mollusc of cool northern coasts. It anchors itself to rocks and to other mussels with tough threads and forms dense beds that shelter many other animals and plants. It is also widely eaten and farmed.

The solid shell is roughly triangular and smooth, with concentric growth lines but no ribs, usually purple or blue and sometimes brown, with a pearl-white interior. Adults are typically 5 to 10 cm, though some populations stay at 2 to 3 cm and the largest reach 15 to 20 cm. It is easily confused with the Mediterranean mussel, and no single feature separates the species reliably.

It lives from the high intertidal zone to shallow subtidal water, roughly 0 to 5 m deep, on open rocky coasts, in crevices, on piers and in estuaries. In the north-east Atlantic it ranges from the White Sea to southern France, and in the west Atlantic from the Canadian Maritimes to North Carolina.
It is a suspension feeder that filters bacteria, phytoplankton, detritus and dissolved organic matter from the water. It can feed only while submerged, so growth is slower higher on the shore.

Mussels are bound together by byssus threads into beds up to five or six layers deep. A detached mussel can make new threads within 24 hours, and several mussels can work together to immobilise a predatory snail with their threads. Settlement of young mussels is gregarious, often among established adults.

Sexes are separate and fertilisation is external, with spawning from April to September, peaking in spring and summer. Females release millions of eggs, up to about 40 million in the largest, and maturity comes at 1 to 2 years. The larvae feed in the plankton for typically 1 to 6 months, and may delay settling for up to 40 days at 10 °C.

Predation is the main cause of death. Dog whelks, starfish, crabs, sea urchins, flatfish and birds such as oystercatchers, eiders and gulls eat mussels, and in the Ythan estuary birds took 72% of annual mussel production. Mussel beds provide hard surface for algae and spaces for worms and other animals, and can host parasites and commensals.

The species is common and abundant in many coastal areas, and the Animal Diversity Web lists no special status. Over-exploitation of small beds can reduce recruitment, and mussels can accumulate pathogens and algal toxins, which matters for people who eat them.

Goldenhead dwarf acara
Nannacara aureocephalus

Nannacara aureocephalus is a small South American cichlid endemic to French Guiana, where records place it in the Approuague drainage. It is a dwarf cichlid, but its restricted natural range and specialist habitat distinguish it from the many aquarium fishes sold under the broad name ‘acara’.

It is a small, laterally compressed cichlid. Adult males grow larger than females; reported standard lengths are about 6.7 cm for males and about 5 cm for females, though measurements and aquarium condition vary. The golden-head common name is a useful field or trade label, not a stand-alone diagnostic: compare the full body pattern, fins, sex and locality with other Nannacara rather than identifying from a yellow head alone.

The species is recorded from the Approuague River basin in French Guiana. Accounts describe shallow water along swamp margins and stagnant sections of forest streams. These quiet, shallow waters are more specific habitat clues than the general label ‘Amazonian freshwater fish’; the available distribution records remain geographically limited.

Species accounts report small invertebrates and insect larvae as important natural foods. This is consistent with a small cichlid foraging among shallow-water vegetation, but the sources do not provide a measured breakdown of prey or seasonal diet.

Its habitat descriptions suggest a fish associated with shallow, slow or still water. Published species summaries available for this profile offer little direct observation of its daily activity, social structure or territorial behavior in the wild, so these are not inferred from better-studied aquarium cichlids.

FishBase reports that the species lays up to about 100 eggs, deposited on the ceiling of a small cave or in the open. The female guards the eggs and young; the source does not describe a corresponding guarding role for the male. This concise account gives a documented pattern, though it does not establish how clutch size or nesting site varies across the species’ limited range.

As a small cichlid feeding on aquatic invertebrates, it is part of the food web of forest streams and swamp margins. No source reviewed here quantifies its ecological role, predators or interactions with other fish, and its narrow known range makes site-specific habitat information especially relevant.

FishBase reports an IUCN global assessment of Least Concern dated 28 December 2020. An older specialist account still says the species had not been assessed, illustrating that some pages have not been updated. The category is dated and does not establish that every local habitat or population is stable; no population trend was verified here.

Mainland clouded leopard
Neofelis nebulosa

The mainland clouded leopard is a medium-sized Asian cat in the genus Neofelis. Genetic and morphological evidence distinguishes it from the Sunda clouded leopard, N. diardi, native to Sumatra and Borneo. Neofelis nebulosa ranges across parts of South and Southeast Asia. Its long tail and cloud-shaped coat are distinctive, but its secretive habits leave much of its biology poorly documented.

Adults have sturdy short legs, broad paws and longer hind legs. Dark-edged, pale-centred blotches mark a yellowish, grey or brown coat; the tail is banded. Nearly as long as the head and body, it helps balance the cat on branches. The skull has exceptionally long upper canines for a living cat. This anatomy alone does not imply unusually large prey: accounts describe a nape bite when it subdues larger animals.

Its range includes Nepal, India, southern China and the Indochinese Peninsula. It is strongly associated with dense evergreen and tropical forests, although secondary and logged forests are also used. Camera-trap surveys in Peninsular Malaysia found local differences in habitat use, including associations with elevation and distance from water; these relationships are not universal habitat requirements.

It takes vertebrate prey on trees and on the ground. Records include macaques, gibbons, muntjacs, pigs, porcupines, pangolins, squirrels and birds. Diet evidence is patchy and varies by site; no comprehensive range-wide study exists. Long canines and climbing ability do not show that arboreal prey dominate. In southern Thailand, muntjacs occupied less disturbed core forest more often, where clouded leopard density was also higher; this local association does not establish cause.

Broad gripping footpads and specialized ankle bones allow varied climbing positions, including descending a trunk headfirst. Direct observations are rare, so one radio-tracking study provides a useful, geographically limited view of movement. In Thailand’s Phu Khieo Wildlife Sanctuary, four cats were tracked for one to 17 months. Their annual ranges measured 22.9–45.1 km², daily travel averaged 1,932 m, and they were active during 58% of recorded diel readings. The small sample cannot establish a universal daily schedule or social pattern.

Most developmental measurements come from captive animals. Smithsonian records report 85–93 days of gestation and one to five cubs, usually two or three. Eyes open around 10–14 days, weaning occurs around 90–100 days, and sexual maturity is reached at about two years. These records do not establish wild reproductive-season or survival averages.

Its role in local food webs is poorly measured. At Khlong Saeng–Khao Sok, Thailand, camera traps recorded at least 27 individuals over 5,242 trap-days. Estimated density was higher in a less accessible forest core than at a more heavily hunted edge. Muntjac occupancy was also higher in the core. These site-specific findings suggest that access, hunting and prey communities may relate to local abundance, but do not establish a universal pattern.

The IUCN Cat Specialist Group cites the 2021 global assessment as Vulnerable. Forest fragmentation, prey depletion, killing and capture for trade threaten the species. Stronghold habitat declined between 2000 and 2018, while population estimates remain uncertain. Conservation priorities include connected forests, reduced snaring and better field surveys.

Nile crocodile
Crocodylus niloticus

The Nile crocodile is a large African crocodilian of rivers, lakes, swamps and estuaries, with a modern range centred in eastern and southern Africa and Madagascar. The Red List’s current taxonomic scope separates it from Crocodylus suchus, the West and Central African species once included in many broad Nile crocodile accounts. It waits at the water’s edge with only its eyes and nostrils exposed, then lunges when prey comes within reach. Fish and other aquatic animals connect its hunting to the food webs of African wetlands.

Its muscular tail supplies the main thrust in water, while strong limbs support movement on land. An Okavango account describes typical adults around 3.5 m long, with males able to reach 5 m. Exceptional males may approach 6 m, an exceptional value rather than a representative adult size. The pointed crocodile muzzle differs from an alligator’s broader one, and its fourth lower tooth remains visible when the jaws close. Eyes, ears and nostrils sit high on the head, and nostrils can close underwater.

The species uses slow and still waters, including rivers, lakes, seasonal swamps, reservoirs and coastal estuaries. It also occurs in desert oasis pools and, in Madagascar, underground streams. Around the Nile, its northernmost modern population is localized at Lake Nasser in Egypt. Older accounts include western populations now assigned to C. suchus.

Its diet changes as it grows. Young juveniles take insects and invertebrates, later adding frogs, crabs, snails, small fish, birds and rodents. Adults eat fish, reptiles, birds and mammals; local prey availability shapes the menu. Large land animals are occasional prey, not the routine food of every large crocodile. It ambushes from water or shore; a crocodile may roll to tear large prey apart.

As an ectotherm, it adjusts body temperature by moving between sunlit banks, shade and water. It often basks by day and spends much of the night in or near water, with activity shifting by weather and season. When submerged, it can expose only its eyes, ears and nostrils and close its nostrils underwater. Nile crocodiles tolerate one another at basking sites, but large males may defend shoreline stretches. Hatchling calls draw adults to the nest and help keep young together.

In local dry seasons, females dig sandy hole nests near permanent water and lay around 40–60 eggs. Incubation commonly lasts about 80–90 days, although temperature changes its duration. Egg temperature also influences sex: one Zimbabwe study produced only females at constant 31 °C or below, while the threshold for males varied among clutches above that range. The female guards the nest and responds to calls from hatching young, uncovering them and carrying hatchlings in her mouth to water. Hatchlings measure about 28 cm and stay guarded in groups for up to three months before dispersing.

In the Okavango Delta, studies describe crocodiles taking fish, recycling nutrients and maintaining wet refuges during drought. Eggs and young also feed other animals: fish, herons, storks, monitor lizards and mammals can prey on them, while larger crocodiles may eat juveniles. These relationships vary by site, water level and life stage, making the crocodile both predator and prey in a changing wetland community.

The global IUCN assessment completed on 30 April 2017 and published in 2019 listed the species as Least Concern, estimating 50,000–70,000 mature individuals. The assessment reports that hunting depleted populations in many countries from the 1940s through the 1960s, while legal protection and CITES trade controls supported recovery in many areas. Habitat conversion, pollution, uncontrolled harvest and conflict killings remain regional pressures; local declines and die-offs are documented within the wider range. Some commercial skins come from ranching or captive breeding, while local harvest still needs careful management in the wild.

Northern Fulmar
Fulmarus glacialis

The northern fulmar looks like a stocky gull but belongs to the tubenoses, the group that includes albatrosses. It spends most of its life at sea and is famous for spitting foul-smelling stomach oil at intruders.

A seabird 45–50 cm long with a wingspan of 102–112 cm. British adults weigh about 770 g and have a wing about 330 mm long. The typical bird is light grey above and white below, with a thick yellow bill whose nostrils form a tube on top. Dark and intermediate colour forms also occur, mainly in Arctic populations.

It feeds over continental-shelf waters from the Arctic to temperate seas, rarely more than 100 km from shore. It breeds on sea cliffs, in Britain around the coasts of Scotland, Wales, Ireland and parts of England where suitable cliffs exist.
It eats fish, squid and large zooplankton such as amphipods, mostly caught at the surface. It is also an opportunistic scavenger of discarded fish and carrion, and often follows fishing boats.

It flies low over the water with stiff wingbeats and long glides. At the nest it defends itself and its site by spitting oil. Young birds spend their first four or five years at sea before visiting colonies.

A pair lays a single egg, incubated for 52–53 days with both sexes taking turns. The chick fledges after about 46–51 days. Fulmars first breed at around nine years of age, and many pairs reuse the same nest site year after year.

Fulmars nest in colonies, often mixed with other seabirds such as kittiwakes. On land, foxes and introduced rats can prey on them. They benefit from fishery discards, which may have helped the North Atlantic population to expand over the past two centuries.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern. The UK breeding population was about 350,000 pairs in 2015; it rose 77% between the 1969–70 and 1985–88 censuses, then fell slightly after the early 2000s, and it is Amber-listed. Fulmars are very long-lived: the oldest ringed bird exceeded 41 years.

Northern gannet
Morus bassanus

The northern gannet is a large seabird of the North Atlantic, breeding on offshore islands and cliffs from northeastern North America to western Europe. It spends much of the year at sea, returning to crowded colonies to nest.

Adults are about 85–100 cm long, with a wingspan of roughly 165–180 cm. The sexes look alike: the body is white, the long narrow wings have black tips, and the head and neck are buff-yellow in breeding plumage. Young birds are dark brown and acquire more white feathers over several years.

Breeding colonies occupy steep sea cliffs, rocky islands and other isolated coastal sites, where many nests fit close together. At sea, gannets range widely over productive shelf waters and follow moving shoals; after breeding, many migrate south within the Atlantic or into the western Mediterranean.

It eats mainly schooling fish, including mackerel, herring and sandeels, as well as squid. From a glide or steep flight it folds its wings and plunges bill-first, often striking at high speed; it can also pursue prey below the surface. Its eyes are protected by a translucent third eyelid, and air spaces beneath the skin cushion the impact. It swallows captured fish underwater or at the surface.

Gannets forage singly or in loose groups, and several birds may dive where fish are driven toward the surface by predators or boats. At colonies, close neighbors defend small nest spaces with upright postures, bill-pointing and harsh calls. Pairs greet with raised bills and mutual display; their repeated calls help maintain contact in the noisy crowd.

Pairs usually return to the same colony and may remain together across years. They build a mound of seaweed, grass and other material, then lay a single egg. Both parents incubate it between their webbed feet for about 42–46 days. The chick hatches helpless and is fed regurgitated fish by both adults; it grows for roughly 84–97 days before its first flight, then leaves the colony and must find food at sea. Breeding generally begins at around five years.

Northern gannets consume schooling pelagic fish and squid, linking their feeding to stocks also sought by commercial fisheries. They can be caught accidentally in fishing nets, so fishing activity affects both their food supply and survival.

The species is globally classified as Least Concern, a status that describes extinction risk across its full range and does not mean every colony is secure. Past egg collection and hunting reduced some colonies, while fishing pressure, bycatch, pollution and changing food supplies remain concerns. Highly pathogenic avian influenza caused severe recent losses: in 2022, at least 11,000 gannet deaths were recorded in Scotland and 5,000 at Grassholm, Wales.

Northern Lapwing
Vanellus vanellus
The northern lapwing is a large plover of farmland and wet grassland, famous for its long crest and its tumbling display flights in spring. Its numbers have fallen steeply across much of Europe.

A lapwing is about 28–31 cm long, and in Britain adults weigh about 250 g with a wing near 231 mm. It has a black crown and breast, white belly, a long wispy crest, and glossy green and purple upperparts that often look black from afar. The under-tail is cinnamon; females have a shorter crest.

It breeds mainly in farmland and agricultural landscapes, favouring wet grasslands, meadows and short grass, often swards kept under 10 cm by grazing cattle. It needs moist soil rich in earthworms and other invertebrates. In winter it feeds more on mudflats at low tide.

It eats earthworms and other invertebrates, with smaller amounts of small fish, seeds and other plant matter. Earthworms and crane-fly larvae are especially important for the chicks, and pastures offer the most earthworms.

Lapwings are territorial and ground-dwelling, and males perform noisy, tumbling song-flights in spring. They nest in loose groups and defend their nests together, using distraction displays and diving at predators. Many birds migrate several thousand kilometres between breeding and wintering areas.

In Britain a clutch is typically four eggs, incubated for about four weeks, mainly by the female. The downy chicks leave the nest soon after hatching and fledge at 35–40 days, and birds typically first breed at two years old. Lost clutches are often replaced.

Eggs are taken by carrion crows, gulls and stoats, while foxes and domestic cats prey on nests and adults. By feeding on soil invertebrates the lapwing may influence their local numbers, and loss of wet, short grassland has been a major pressure on the species.

The species is classed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List and Vulnerable in Europe, and it is Red-listed in the UK. Britain’s breeding population was about 98,000 pairs in 2016, down 65% since 1967. The oldest ringed bird lived over 21 years.

Northern Pintail
Anas acuta
The northern pintail is an elegant dabbling duck, slightly bigger than a Mallard, with a long neck and a small head. In Britain it is mainly a winter visitor, and breeding there is rare.

In Britain adult males average about 1,030 g with a wing of 277 mm; females are smaller, about 819 g and 259 mm. Both sexes have a long, slender, dark grey bill. The male has a chocolate-brown head, a creamy throat and a long central tail feather of up to about 10 cm. In flight the curved back, pointed wings and tapering tail are distinctive.

In winter it favours sheltered coasts, grazing marshes, river floodplains and estuaries. Breeding in Britain is localised, mainly on the coast of East Anglia and in the northern and western isles of Scotland. Elsewhere it uses marshes, ponds, lakes and flooded grain fields.
The pintail is omnivorous. It eats grain and wild seeds, aquatic plant roots, insects, small crustaceans and snails, reaching food in deeper water by upending, helped by its longer neck.

It is social and migratory, often mixing with other waterfowl, and can cover long distances quickly. In Britain it is a locally common winter visitor, present from late August to May. In courtship the males whistle and display to the females.

In Britain a pair raises one brood a year. The female lays typically 7–9 eggs and incubates them alone for 22–24 days. The precocial ducklings feed themselves soon after hatching and fledge after roughly 40–45 days. Breeding usually starts at one year of age.

The pintail feeds on seeds, plants and small invertebrates and is itself prey for foxes, coyotes and other predators; crows, gulls, skunks and foxes take its eggs. It is a quarry species in winter, though in Britain shooting does not appear to affect its population status.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern, but it is Vulnerable in Europe and Amber-listed in the UK. About 27 pairs bred in the UK in 2013–17 and some 20,000 birds winter there; the winter population fell by 6% between 1998 and 2023. The typical life expectancy is about three years.

Eurasian Curlew
Numenius arquata

The Eurasian curlew is the largest European wading bird, known for its long, down-curved bill and its bubbling, far-carrying call over moorland and estuaries. It is now a species of high conservation concern, with steep declines across much of its range.

A curlew measures 50–60 cm, with a wingspan around 90 cm, and weighs roughly 770 g to 1 kg; females are larger than males and have longer bills. The plumage is mottled brown and grey, the legs long and bluish, and in flight a white wedge shows on the rump.

In the breeding season in Britain it is most frequent on moorland and also common in marshes, using upland rough pasture, heather moor, bogs and wet grassland. In winter it moves to the coast and nearby farmland, with the highest densities on major estuaries.

It finds worms, shellfish and shrimps by probing the ground with the sensitive tip of its long bill. It pinches the prey and often tosses it into the air before swallowing, because its tongue cannot reach far enough to move it.

Its “cur-lee” and bubbling calls are heard over breeding grounds from February to July. From July many birds move to the coast, where they roost in flocks at high tide and feed on the mudflats at low tide. British winter flocks are joined by migrants from Fennoscandia.

In Britain the first clutch is laid on average around 2 May, typically four eggs, with one brood. The female, and occasionally the male, incubates for 27–29 days. The downy chicks run soon after hatching and fledge after 32–38 days. Breeding typically starts at two years of age.

Nest predation is a major problem: egg predation caused nest failure in up to 97% of nests in a Northern Ireland study in the 1990s, and foxes were the main cause in a Breckland study. Predator control raised success in one Northumberland site, though the effect of some predators appears to depend on the place. Changing farm practices and loss of breeding and chick-rearing habitat also contribute to the decline.

The IUCN lists the species as Near Threatened. The UK breeding population was about 59,000 pairs in 2016 and fell by 51% between 1995 and 2024; the UK is thought to hold over 30% of the west European population, and the species is Red-listed in the UK. A curlew typically lives about 11 years once adult, and the oldest ringed bird reached over 32.

Kozlov’s Pika
Ochotona koslowi

Kozlov’s pika is a rare pika living only in the high mountains of western China. It was collected in 1884 and described in 1894, then went unseen by scientists for about a century until its rediscovery in 1984. It is listed as Endangered, largely because so little is known about it.

A medium-sized pika with a body of 170–240 mm and a weight of 100–300 g. White lips and an almost cubic skull set it apart from the Ladakh pika and the plateau pika, two species it can be mistaken for: some museum specimens labelled as Kozlov’s pika actually belong to those species.

It lives in alpine grassland and mountain steppe at about 4,100–4,800 m, on high, isolated mountains near the meeting point of Qinghai, Xinjiang and Tibet. Records come from the Kunlun Mountains, the Kongka mountains and the Aerjin Mountain Nature Reserve. The first animals, in 1884, were found in burrows dug in mounds of salty loess. Its range is very fragmented, with about 800 km between some subpopulations.
It eats green plants, and 15 plant species have been recorded in its diet. No hay-making has been documented for it.

It is active by day and lives in communal family groups, in burrows with several entrances. Densities of roughly 300–400 animals per km² have been reported, but the sources warn that some older studies may have involved other pika species, so these figures deserve caution.
Little is known. Litters of 4–8 embryos have been recorded and a second breeding in the same season has been reported. Gestation, weaning and lifespan are not documented in the sources read.
Its role in its ecosystem has not been studied. It is probably a sister species of the Ladakh pika and may be an ancestral lineage in decline, according to a review of the genus.

It is listed as Endangered because little is known about its distribution and abundance. Little new information has appeared since 1998, and its current status is unknown at two of its three known locations. A climate model has predicted a decrease in the species, with no date given. More fieldwork is needed to plan its protection.

Northern Wheatear
Oenanthe oenanthe

The northern wheatear is a small, mainly ground-dwelling chat of open country, and one of the great long-distance migrants among small birds. It arrives in Britain in spring from Africa and leaves again at the end of summer.

About the size of a robin, an adult weighs roughly 28 g with a wing length near 10 cm. The male has a blue-grey back, black wings, a black cheek patch with a white eyestripe, and a white underside flushed orange on the breast. The female is sandy brown. Both sexes show a white rump and a black T-shaped mark on the tail in flight.

In the breeding season in Britain it is most frequent on moorland, and it is found more widely in open uplands, pasture, heathland and coasts, including Scotland’s outlying islands. Its main strongholds are in Scotland, northern and south-west England and Wales.
The wheatear eats insects, their larvae and other invertebrates, and it also takes berries. It feeds on the ground, where it hops or runs across short vegetation to pick up its prey.

It is a summer visitor to Britain that winters in Africa, arriving around March and leaving in September and October. Birds breeding in Greenland and Alaska also pass through; some fly non-stop across the Atlantic to northern Spain before continuing to West Africa. On the ground it hops or runs.

In Britain the first clutch is laid on average around 11 May, typically five or six eggs, incubated for about 14 days mainly by the female. The chicks fledge after roughly 15.5–16.5 days. There are usually two broods and occasionally three. The nest is placed in a sheltered cavity such as a rock crevice, rabbit burrow or hole in a wall.
As an insect eater of open uplands, the wheatear feeds on ground invertebrates, and in turn it can be taken by birds of prey such as the sparrowhawk.

The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern worldwide. In the UK it is Amber-listed: the breeding population was about 170,000 pairs in 2016 and fell by 37% between 1995 and 2024. Numbers have also declined across Europe since 1980. A wheatear typically lives about two years, and the oldest ringed bird reached over eight.

Okapi
Okapia johnstoni

The okapi is a forest-dwelling giraffid native to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its short neck and compact body contrast with the tall giraffe, its closest living relative. Pale bands on the hindquarters and legs do not make it a relative of zebras.

Adults have a sturdy body, sloping back, short neck and upright ears. The torso is dark brown to reddish; cream-white bands cross the rump and upper legs. Males bear two short, skin-covered ossicones; females lack them. Both sexes use a long dark tongue to grasp leaves and ruminate.

Its known range is northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, including Ituri. It inhabits dense tropical forest. The IUCN assessment records it from about 450 to 1,500 metres elevation. The Okapi Wildlife Reserve protects a major part of Ituri forest.

This browser eats leaves, buds and shoots from shrubs and low branches, as well as fruit and fungi. The Okapi Conservation Project reports leaves from over one hundred plant and tree species in its diet. Foods vary by place and season. Okapis also eat clay or soil, probably for minerals, though its nutritional role is uncertain.

Okapis are usually solitary; females stay with calves. Adults may use overlapping areas, while males can exclude other males. Foot glands leave scent traces; males also mark with urine. Calls include coughs, bleats and whistles. Very low calls have been linked to mother–calf communication, though their function remains uncertain.

Gestation lasts about fourteen to sixteen months; births are usually single. Calves resemble adults and stand soon after birth. A mother may leave a calf hidden while feeding, then return to nurse. Young sample solid food within weeks. Maturity near three years is reported mainly from managed animals.

Okapis browse forest vegetation and are prey for leopards. Conservation programmes use this distinctive animal as an emblem for protecting the Ituri forest, benefiting other species sharing its habitat.

The 2015 IUCN assessment classified the okapi as Endangered, estimating a decline over 50% across three generations. This is the assessment date, not a new 2026 measurement. Pressures include poaching, forest loss and degradation, and insecurity. The Ituri reserve and local conservation programs support protection.

King Cobra
Ophiophagus hannah

The king cobra is the world’s longest venomous snake, living in the forests of South and Southeast Asia. Its scientific name means snake-eater: it feeds mainly on other snakes. It is also the only snake known to build a nest, which the female guards.

Adults usually measure about 3–4 m, and the longest known individual was 5.85 m. Adults are olive, brown, yellow or nearly black, often with pale cross-bars or chevrons, and the throat is light yellow or cream. When threatened it raises the front of the body and spreads its hood. Juveniles are black with yellow or white cross-bars.

It ranges from northern India east to southern China and south through the Malay Peninsula to western Indonesia and the Philippines. It lives near streams in dense or open forest, in bamboo thickets, nearby farmland and dense mangroves. In Bhutan, one survey recorded it between 650 and 2,057 m, mostly lower, and mainly where human disturbance was low.

It feeds mainly on other snakes, including large and mostly harmless species such as Asian rat snakes and pythons, as well as other cobras and kraits. Some individuals eat only one species of snake. When food is scarce, it may also take lizards, birds and other small vertebrates.

It is active by day and usually retreats rather than attack, but it defends a nest fiercely. In a threat display it raises the front of the body about a metre off the ground, spreads its hood, hisses loudly and can strike from a distance. Its venom is a powerful neurotoxin that can cause death by respiratory failure.

It breeds from January to April. The female pushes leaves and branches into a pile and lays her eggs in it, and the heat of decay incubates them. Clutches have about 21–40 eggs in one source and 7–43 in another, with incubation of roughly 66 to 105 days. She guards the nest, often from on top of it, while the male stays nearby, and females can be very aggressive towards intruders.

As an apex predator that eats mainly other snakes, the king cobra is placed high in forest food webs. In a Bhutan study, a nest of 37 eggs was monitored and found to be guarded by the female. It is also a popular display animal in zoos.

The king cobra is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List and is in CITES Appendix II. The main threats are habitat destruction and persecution by people who fear snakes. It is protected by law in several countries, including China, Vietnam and India.

Orca
Orcinus orca

The orca, or killer whale, is the largest member of the dolphin family. It occurs in every ocean, from polar waters to the tropics. Its species-wide range contains distinct populations whose diets, calls and social traditions vary considerably.

A robust, streamlined body carries sharply contrasting black and white markings, including pale oval eye patches and a grey saddle behind the dorsal fin. The rounded head has no distinct beak; a tall fin, especially in adult males, helps identify the species.

Orcas inhabit coastal seas, continental shelves and open ocean across all major ocean basins. They are most abundant in colder regions but also occur in tropical and subtropical waters. Some communities range widely offshore; others use coastal corridors, and ranges can overlap.

Food choice differs among populations and is often shaped by learned hunting traditions. In the northeast Pacific, resident communities mainly take fish, including salmon; Bigg’s whales hunt marine mammals, while offshore whales eat fish and sharks. Elsewhere, prey includes herring, rays, seals or penguins.

Many orcas maintain long-lasting, often maternally related social groups. Clicks, whistles and pulsed calls coordinate activity and keep groups in contact; call repertoires can be learned and shared within communities. Some populations cooperate during hunts, but group size and social structure vary.

Females mature at roughly 10–13 years and carry a single calf for about 15–18 months. A calf nurses for at least a year and remains close to its mother for two years or longer. Births occur throughout the year; intervals differ among populations.

As a predator, an orca can influence prey abundance and behaviour, depending on local food webs and hunting traditions. It also transfers energy and nutrients through the marine food web. Persistent pollutants accumulate in its blubber over a long life.

Risk is uneven: some local populations face depleted prey, fishing-gear entanglement, vessel disturbance and underwater noise, while contaminants can affect health and reproduction. The IUCN’s 2017 global assessment classed the species Data Deficient, reflecting limited population-wide information, not proof that every population is secure.

Spotted Wobbegong
Orectolobus maculatus

The spotted wobbegong is a flattened carpet shark of the coastal waters of southern and eastern Australia. It spends the day motionless on the bottom and hunts at night, relying on camouflage and ambush rather than speed.

The head is flat and fringed on each side with 6–10 branched, fleshy lobes. The body is yellowish to greenish-brown with large dark saddles and whitish O-shaped rings, and there are two dorsal fins but no fin spines. Most adults measure 150–180 cm, though the maximum is cited as about 320 cm, and newborns are about 21–23 cm.

It lives on the continental shelf from the intertidal zone to about 218 m, mostly in shallow water, on rocky and coral reefs, sand, seagrass beds and under piers. Its range runs from Queensland around southern Australia to Western Australia; records from Japan and the South China Sea are probably misidentifications.

It eats bottom invertebrates such as crabs, lobsters and octopuses, and bony fishes including sea basses, scorpionfishes and luderick. Smaller sharks are also taken. It catches prey by sucking it in with a sudden opening of the jaws.

It is sluggish and often rests on the sea floor for long periods, mostly in daytime. The fringe of lobes around its head breaks up its outline and acts as a lure, and prey sometimes nibble it before being seized. It looks docile but can bite hard if provoked or stepped on, and often does not let go.

It is ovoviviparous: the eggs develop inside the female, and the young are born independent. Litters reach up to 37 pups after a gestation of 10–11 months, with births in spring. Females have a cycle of about three years, and males hold a female by biting near her gills during mating.

As a nocturnal ambush predator with a trophic level of about 4.2, it feeds on both invertebrates and fishes of reefs and sand. It carries many parasites, including 33 species of tapeworm reported in one account.

The IUCN lists it as Least Concern (assessed 2015, as reported by FishBase). It is caught as bycatch in trawls and lobster pots and by spearfishing. In New South Wales, trawling caused declines in the early 1990s and the species was listed as Vulnerable there; numbers later stabilised, and bag and size limits now apply to recreational fishing.

Common ostrich
Struthio camelus
The common ostrich is the largest living bird, a flightless inhabitant of Africa’s open landscapes. Its long stride is carried by a two-toed foot whose large inner toe bears most of its weight.

Adult males are larger on average: the Paris Muséum gives females as 1.75–1.90 metres tall and 90–110 kilograms, and males as 2.10–2.75 metres and 100–150 kilograms. Males have black plumage with white wing and tail feathers; females are grey-brown. Each foot has two toes, a large clawed inner toe and a smaller outer toe. Pressure recordings show that the main toe bears most of the load, while the mobile outer toe helps balance the foot during walking and running. In laboratory trials, two adult females ran at 3–6 m/s; the study did not test a maximum speed.
It uses open savannas, grasslands and dry scrub, including places with sparse or short vegetation. Sparse plants leave open sightlines. The species occurs across much of Africa.

Leaves, roots, flowers and seeds make up much of the diet; ostriches also take insects and other small animals. Food is swallowed whole. In adult domesticated birds, a study describes pebbles grinding food in the muscular gizzard and microbial fermentation in the caeca and colon. These digestive observations come from managed birds; wild food choices vary with local and seasonal plant growth.

Ostriches are social ground-dwellers. Groups loosen outside breeding and become more organized around territorial males during courtship; reported flock sizes vary with place and season. Males court with bows, wing movements and conspicuous feathers, accompanied by calls. Although flightless, it uses its wings while running to help change direction, and fans them in hot weather to help keep cool.

Breeding arrangements vary among populations. In East Africa, several hens laid in one shallow scrape; a field report describes communal nests holding 30–40 eggs of about 1.5 kilograms each. Genetic work in Nairobi found multiple mothers and fathers among eggs in the same nest. A dominant hen and territorial male guard and incubate; the female’s pale plumage blends by day and the male’s dark plumage by night. San Diego Zoo gives 42–46 days for incubation. Chicks leave within days, follow adults and are sheltered from sun, rain and predators. Their patterned down is replaced as adult feathers develop; the zoo account says they near adult size at about six months. Adult size precedes sexual maturity, which the Smithsonian account places around three to four years.

Ostriches move nomadically as rainfall changes the availability of fresh plant food. A South African field guide reports that breeding and laying precede rains, so chicks hatch as forage becomes available. In northern Tanzania, surveys of the Masai population found local ostrich densities correlated with those of nine of ten large ungulate species, although their site-specific population trends were not closely correlated. Ostriches themselves are prey for large carnivores, including lions, cheetahs, leopards and hyenas.

BirdLife International’s 2025 global IUCN assessment lists the common ostrich as Least Concern, with a decreasing population trend. This global category does not describe the condition of every regional population. Northern Sahel transects repeated in 1971–73 and 2004 documented severe regional declines and identified hunting, overgrazing and woodland degradation among local pressures. Historic feather hunting and egg collection also affected ostriches, while habitat loss remains a concern.

Fat-tailed Gerbil
Pachyuromys duprasi

The fat-tailed gerbil is a small rodent of the northern Sahara and the only species in its genus. It was first described in 1880 from Laghouat, in Algeria. It is listed as Least Concern and is best known for its short, swollen tail.

A round-bodied gerbil with a head and body of about 108 mm and a weight near 36 g. The long, fluffy fur is grey to tan, with a white belly and feet. The eyes are large and oval and the pink ears sit low on the head. The tail is shorter than the body, thick and club-shaped, without a tuft, and stores fat and water.

It lives in sand sheets with some vegetation, and sometimes in rocky desert. The Mammal Diversity Database gives its range as the northern Sahara from Western Sahara and Morocco to northern Egypt, while Animal Diversity Web describes it mainly west of the Nile Delta, into Libya, Tunisia and Algeria. It digs burrows up to about 1 m deep and sometimes uses those of other rodents.
In the wild it is mostly insectivorous, but it also eats plants, such as the desert shrubs Anabasis articulata and Artemisia monosperma.

It is mainly nocturnal, though often active at dusk, and spends much of its life in burrows. It is found in colonies but can also live alone. Males mark territory with scent glands on the belly. It is docile when handled and rarely bites, but can be aggressive toward others of its own species.

Gestation lasts 19–22 days and a litter holds 3–9 young, 4.5 on average; up to three litters a year are possible. Young are born blind and naked, are cared for by the female alone and are weaned at 3–4 weeks. Maturity comes at 3–6 months. Much of this information comes from captive animals and mostly from the Egyptian subspecies.

Its digging may aerate desert soil, and it probably affects local insect and plant populations. Birds are likely predators, but predation is poorly documented. The pale fur and the burrowing habit may help it avoid predators.
It is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. The sources read give no population estimate and no specific threat for wild animals.

Common Palm Civet
Paradoxurus hermaphroditus

The common palm civet is a nocturnal, tree-dwelling carnivoran of the civet family that lives in the forests of southern and south-eastern Asia and has adapted well to gardens, plantations and villages. It eats mostly fruit despite belonging to the order Carnivora.

A slender civet weighing about 1.3 to 5 kg, with a head and body of roughly 43–71 cm and a tail almost as long as the body, tipped with black but without rings. The coat is short and coarse, grey to blackish, with black-tipped guard hairs, dark stripes down the back and rows of black spots along the flanks. White patches on the face give it a masked look.

It lives in tropical and temperate forests and also in parks, suburban gardens, orchards and plantations, preferring tall trees with dense canopy and vines. It rests by day in tree hollows, rock crevices or thick foliage, and is recorded from sea level to about 2,000 m.

It is an opportunistic omnivore that leans heavily on fruit. In a secondary forest in West Java, fruit and seeds occurred in almost all droppings (97.6 %), animal remains in about a fifth. In an Indian sanctuary in winter, insects were the most frequent item in droppings, followed by fig fruit, birds and rodents.

Mostly solitary and active at night, it climbs trees to feed and rests in them by day. It stalks and pounces on animal prey. It is generally silent, snarling or hissing when alarmed, and marks surfaces with scent from a gland near the base of the tail.

Breeding can occur year-round, with up to two litters a year. After a gestation of about two months, a litter of two to five young is born, often in a tree hollow or rock crevice. Eyes open at about 11 days, young are weaned around two months and independent at about three months, according to a university database.

By eating fruit and passing seeds, it acts as a seed disperser: seeds of at least eight plant species were found in its droppings in West Java, and palm seeds are deposited far from the parent tree. It also eats rodents, and is preyed on by large cats, big snakes and crocodiles.

The Mammal Diversity Database lists it as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. Animal Diversity Web reports legal protection in India and some other regions and names logging and forest clearing for oil palm plantations as threats. Taxonomy is under revision: the database now treats the species in a narrower sense than before, so older figures may cover several species.

Marbled Cat
Pardofelis marmorata

The marbled cat is a small forest cat of South and South-East Asia, about the size of a house cat, with a long tail and a coat marked like that of a clouded leopard. It is rarely seen and poorly studied, and is listed as Near Threatened.

A cat with a body of 45–61 cm, a tail of 35–55 cm and a weight of 2.4–5 kg. The coat is yellowish brown with large blotches, paler in the centre and outlined in black, and black lines on the head, neck and back. The tail is spotted, black at the tip and usually held horizontally when walking. The ears are short and rounded, the feet large and the canines big for its size. Young are mottled brown until about four months.

It depends on forest and has not been found inside oil palm plantations. It is recorded in mixed deciduous-evergreen forest, secondary and logged forest, from sea level to about 3,000 m. Its range runs from the eastern Himalayan foothills through mainland South-East Asia to Sumatra and Borneo; its presence in Bangladesh and Bhutan is uncertain.

Its diet is poorly known. Birds, up to the size of a pheasant, are thought to be the main prey, along with tree squirrels, tree shrews, rodents, small primates, fruit bats, lizards, frogs and insects. This rests on few observations, such as a cat seen stalking birds in the canopy.

It is solitary and a skilled climber, able to come down tree trunks head first, but it is not limited to trees and also walks on the ground. It was long thought to be nocturnal, yet camera traps and sightings show activity by day as well as by night. One radio-collared female in Thailand used a range of about 5.3 km², a single animal that cannot stand for the species.

Nearly everything known comes from captivity: gestation of 66–82 days and litters of 2–4 kittens, usually two. Eyes open at about 16 days, kittens walk at about 22 days, eat solid food around 59 days and females mature at 21–22 months. The female raises the young alone. Breeding has not been documented in the wild.

It is a predator of birds and small mammals. No predator of the marbled cat is documented. In three Sabah study areas in Borneo, camera traps gave densities of 7.1 (upland primary forest), 10.5 (logged lowland forest) and 19.6 (lowland primary forest) animals per 100 km²; the authors suggest these may be at the high end of the species’ abundance.

It is listed as Near Threatened since 2015, having been Vulnerable in 2008; this change does not mean its numbers have risen or its threats lessened, as the species is still poorly studied. Forest loss is the main threat, and indiscriminate snaring is probably a major one. It is in CITES Appendix I.

Eurasian Tree Sparrow
Passer montanus

The Eurasian tree sparrow is a small, sociable sparrow of farmland edges. In Britain it has suffered a severe long-term decline, and it is a Red-listed species there despite a recent small recovery from a very low level.

Slightly smaller than a house sparrow, an adult weighs about 21 g and has a wing length near 70 mm. It has a chestnut crown and nape, white cheeks with a black spot, a small black bib and a streaky brown back. Males and females look alike, and juveniles resemble faded adults.

In Britain and Ireland it lives mainly in eastern and lowland areas and is most frequent on arable farmland in the breeding season. In winter it gathers in flocks on stubble fields and sometimes visits garden feeders in rural villages.

It eats seeds of grasses and weeds and cultivated grain such as barley and wheat, and catches small insects to feed its young. Chicks fed more seed and fewer invertebrates fledged less successfully in one study.

It is social, breeding in small loose colonies, and shyer and less boisterous than the house sparrow, often holding its tail up. Outside the breeding season it can travel considerable distances, and some breeding areas are vacated entirely in winter.

It nests in holes and crevices in buildings, banks, cliffs and nest boxes. The breeding season runs from April to August, with one or two broods of typically five or six eggs. Both sexes incubate for 12–13 days, and the chicks fledge after about 15–17.5 days. Breeding typically starts at one year.

Breeding success is linked to the invertebrate prey fed to the chicks, and in winter birds gather where seed food is available. A typical adult lives about two years, and the oldest ringed bird reached nearly eleven.

The IUCN Red List classes it as Least Concern, but in the UK it is Red-listed. UK numbers fell by an estimated 93% between 1970 and 2008; the breeding population was 245,000 territories in 2016, up 18% since 1995 but far below 1970s levels. In Europe it has declined since 1980.

Edible Frog
Pelophylax esculentus

The edible frog is a green water frog of central and north-eastern Europe. It is not a true species in the usual sense but a fertile hybrid between the pool frog and the marsh frog, which keeps going by mating with one of its parents.

It reaches up to 12 cm but is mostly under 10 cm, females being larger. The back is light to dark green or brownish with dark spots, often with a light green stripe down the middle, and the backs of the thighs are yellowish or orange with dark bars. The skin is usually smooth and the hind legs long and well webbed. Males have grey nuptial pads on the thumbs and white to grey vocal sacs.

It uses many sun-exposed waters with well-overgrown margins and shallows, from woodland ponds to ditches, lakes and rivers, sometimes in brackish water. It ranges across mid and north-eastern Europe as far as Russia. Introduced colonies in southern England probably all came from releases.

In mixed water frog populations studied in Serbia, insects made up about 88% of the prey items found in stomachs, mostly Hymenoptera, beetles, Lepidoptera and flies. Frogs are opportunistic hunters and their diet varies from site to site. It forages on land mainly at night.

It stays mostly in water and basks a lot. It is mainly active by day but also at night during the breeding season, when males call in dense groups, chiefly in the evening, with grunting or rattling notes. It usually hibernates in soil on land, sometimes underwater, and young frogs can travel several kilometres.

Frogs leave hibernation from about mid-March and eggs are laid from April to mid-July, mostly around mid-May. A female lays 3,000 to 8,000 eggs per season. Tadpoles need two to four months to develop, most transforming between mid-August and mid-September, and frogs mature after two to three years.

The edible frog reproduces by hybridogenesis: it passes on one parental genome unchanged and so needs a parent species to mate with. In the common arrangement it mates with the pool frog, in another with the marsh frog. Some populations are made up only of hybrids, with diploid and triploid frogs together.

It is often the most numerous green frog where it occurs. The sources read give no Red List category for this hybrid. In Serbia, mixed populations of the three water frog forms are rare and only found along the Danube.

Grey Partridge
Perdix perdix

The grey partridge is a plump, ground-living gamebird of European farmland. Once very common and widespread, it has suffered serious declines across most of its range and is now a conservation concern in the UK.

An adult weighs about 390 g with a wing length near 16 cm. The plumage is finely barred grey and brown, with an orange face and throat, chestnut bars on the flanks and a chestnut tail. Males are larger and usually show a U-shaped chestnut patch on the belly; females are duller, with a smaller patch or none.

It is a resident, sedentary bird of lowland farmland, most frequent on arable land in the breeding season. It needs open fields for feeding by day and dense cover to hide in and nest. Chicks depend on cover and on invertebrates, even on rough grazing on hill farms in north-east England.

Adults eat mainly seeds, grain, leaves, roots and shoots, with cereals important in the warmer months. Chicks, in contrast, need protein and feed on insects, including sawfly larvae in a north-east England study, and aphids.

A strictly ground-living bird, it spends the non-breeding season in groups called coveys, usually of 6 to 15 birds and sometimes up to 25, often made up of relatives. Members feed and roost together and keep watch for danger. When threatened, the birds run or fly low and fast, and their bodies can look like clods of earth.

In the UK there is typically one brood a year, with a very large clutch of 13–16 eggs, sometimes more than 20. The female alone incubates for 23–25 days. The downy chicks leave the nest at once and can fly short distances at about two weeks old. Breeding typically starts at one year of age.

Birds of prey such as goshawks and sparrowhawks, and ground predators such as foxes, take adults, eggs and chicks, and higher predation lowers nest success and winter survival. The main driver of decline is agricultural intensification, especially the loss of chick food through pesticide and herbicide use. The birds also disperse seeds in their droppings.

The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern worldwide, but it has declined across Europe. In the UK it is Red-listed: the breeding population was about 37,000 territories in 2016 and fell by 93% between 1967 and 2024. It typically lives about three years once adult, and the oldest ringed bird reached over five.
